client: Lately, I've been feeling completely burnt out trying to keep my grades perfect while working 20 hours a week at the campus library. I know I should be able to handle this, but I keep having these moments where I just freeze up when I look at my to-do list. Honestly, I'm not even sure talking about it will help - it's not like my deadlines or bills are going away.
therapist: It sounds like you're carrying a heavy load of responsibilities while also being really hard on yourself. I notice you say "I should be able to handle this" - what would it feel like to acknowledge that what you're managing is genuinely a lot?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, very quiet, moderate-paced speech

client: I guess admitting it's a lot makes me feel... I don't know, weak maybe? Like I'm making excuses. My roommate takes more credits and works full-time, so why can't I handle this? The thought of acknowledging it's too much makes my chest get tight - like then I'd have to change something.
therapist: It sounds like you're comparing yourself harshly while also experiencing very real physical tension. What would you say to a friend who was feeling this same way about their workload?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client: I'd probably tell my friend they're pushing themselves too hard and need to cut back somewhere. But when it's me... I don't know, it feels different. Like if I ease up even a little, everything will fall apart. And honestly? The thought of saying "no" to anything makes me more anxious than just powering through.
therapist: It seems like there's a gap between what you'd advise a friend and how you treat yourself - that's really common when we're being self-critical. What feels most important to explore right now: the fear of everything falling apart, or the anxiety around saying "no"?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: I think it's the fear of everything falling apart that really gets me. Like if I drop one ball, the whole juggling act will collapse. I have this image in my head of my professors being disappointed, my boss thinking I'm unreliable... it's like one small mistake will prove I'm actually not capable after all.
therapist: Your voice sounds quieter as you describe this fear - it seems to really weigh on you. That image of everything collapsing if you make one mistake - could we examine whether that thought might be predicting more catastrophe than what realistically happens?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client: Well... I guess I did have to miss a shift last semester when I had the flu, and my boss was actually pretty understanding about it. But that feels different - that was a real emergency. If I just say "I can't handle this", that feels like I'm failing by choice.
therapist: It's interesting how you separate "real emergencies" from needing to set boundaries - as if your wellbeing only counts when your body forces you to stop. I notice you're speaking quickly when you describe this - what comes up when you imagine giving yourself permission to set limits before reaching crisis point?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client: When you put it that way... I can see how I only let myself stop when I physically can't go on. Imagining setting limits before that point makes me feel guilty, like I'm taking the easy way out. But I'm also scared because I know I can't keep going like this forever - I'm already so tired all the time.
therapist: You're holding two important realizations here - both the guilt about setting boundaries and the awareness that this pace isn't sustainable. That sounds like a painful tension to sit with. What would happen if we looked at self-care not as "the easy way out," but as what allows you to keep going in a healthier way?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client: That... actually makes me tear up a little. I've never thought of it like that before. But part of me is still resistant - if I start prioritizing self-care now, won't I just get lazy? Like maybe I'll lose my drive completely if I let up even a little.
therapist: It's understandable to worry that self-care might make you lose your edge - that fear comes through clearly in how quickly you're speaking. What if we explored what "lazy" really means to you? Where do you think that fear comes from?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, very rapid speech

client: I think it goes back to high school when my dad would say "only the lazy take breaks" while I was studying. Now even taking a 15-minute break feels like failure. But when I say it out loud, it sounds kind of extreme... I just can't shake the feeling that if I'm not pushing myself constantly, I'll turn into someone who doesn't achieve anything.
therapist: It sounds like your father's words still have a powerful hold on how you view productivity and self-worth. Now that you hear how extreme that belief sounds out loud, what thoughts come up about whether "only the lazy take breaks" might need updating?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client: I know logically that breaks are important - we even learned about productivity studies in psych class. But emotionally, it still feels wrong. Like if I start believing breaks are okay, I'm just making excuses for myself. I can feel my shoulders tensing up just thinking about it.
therapist: I hear both the logical understanding about breaks and the physical tension that comes when you consider actually taking them. That gap between knowing something intellectually and feeling it emotionally can be so frustrating. Where do you think that deep-seated belief that breaks equal excuses comes from?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client: I think it comes from seeing my dad work himself to the bone growing up - he never took vacations and would work through illnesses. I internalized that as what being a "good worker" looks like, but now that I'm actually living it... I feel trapped. Like I can't break this pattern even though it's making me miserable.
therapist: You've connected this pattern back to your father's example - that seems like such an important insight. I hear how painful it is to realize you've adopted an approach to work that's making you miserable, even as part of you still believes it's the "right" way. What might it feel like to start defining for yourself what being a "good worker" really means?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech
